name: Ways a tape was merged
brief:
Two feeds `a` and `b` were merged into one string `tape` by a process that keeps each feed's letters in order. Nobody logged which letter came from which feed.

Write `merge_ways(a, b, tape)`, which returns the number of ways to share out the letters of `tape` between the two feeds so that they spell `a` and `b` in order, modulo 1,000,000,007. Two ways differ when some position of `tape` goes to a different feed. If `tape` cannot be made this way, the answer is 0. Empty `a`, `b` and `tape` give 1: there is one way to share out nothing.

Example. For `a = 'ab'`, `b = 'a'` and `tape = 'aab'`, the letter from `b` can be the first or the second `a` of the tape, so the answer is 2.
constraints: `a` and `b` hold $0$ to $150$ lower-case letters each, and `tape` holds $0$ to $300$.
$O(|a| \cdot |b|)$ time is the target. Recursing on which feed gave the next letter, without remembering answers, is too slow.
All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: Check the lengths first. Cell `(i, j)` counts the ways to make the first `i + j` letters of the tape from the first `i` of `a` and the first `j` of `b`; its last letter came from `a[i - 1]` or from `b[j - 1]`.

examples.note: The `b` of the tape must come from `a`, and either `a` before it can be the one from `b`.
Only one sharing works: `x` and `y` from `a`, `z` from `b`.
The tape has five letters but the feeds have four, so no sharing exists.

tests.call: merge_ways(''.join('ab'[(i * i) % 7 % 2] for i in range(150)), ''.join('ab'[(i * 3) % 5 % 2] for i in range(150)), ''.join('ab'[(i * i) % 7 % 2] for i in range(75)) + ''.join('ab'[(i * 3) % 5 % 2] for i in range(150)) + ''.join('ab'[(i * i) % 7 % 2] for i in range(75, 150)))

how: Submit runs 15 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value. The obvious method recurses on which feed gave the next letter without remembering answers, and on long runs of one letter both choices match at every step, so it runs out of time. The step to the target is a table over the number of letters used from each feed. Unlike asking whether the tape is a merge of the two feeds, this counts the merges, so both matching moves are added rather than either one taken.
notes: Cell `(i, j)` counts the ways to make the first `i + j` letters of the tape from the first `i` of `a` and the first `j` of `b`.
When the next letters of both feeds match the tape, both moves count, so a yes-or-no merge check undercounts.
The table has $(|a| + 1)(|b| + 1)$ cells, each filled in $O(1)$, so the work is $O(|a| \cdot |b|)$.

planted.slip: Recording only whether a merge exists answers 1 where several sharings work.
Skipping the length check counts sharings of the first letters of a tape that is too long for the two feeds.
Leaving out the modulus returns the full count, which for long runs of one letter has well over eighty digits.
Recursing on which feed gave the next letter is right but repeats the same pair of positions again and again.
